intro: Chapter 2 turns the verb into three new tools: one that says “having done”, one that says “to do”, and one that says “who is doing”. With them, short sentences grow into natural, flowing Pāli.

blocks.html: So far every verb was finite: it had a subject and an ending (gacchati). The forms in this chapter are non-finite: they are built from a verb but do not act as the main verb. They hang additional actions onto a sentence.
Gerund and infinitive are indeclinable. The participle is an adjective, so it takes case and number endings, exactly like the nouns from Chapter 1.

blocks.title: Formation
formulas: prefixed verbs often use -ya | āgamma, ādāya, āruyha

items: Decide the main action and its subject: Naro … bhuñjati.
Did something happen first by the same person? Add a gerund phrase before the main verb: gehaṃ gantvā.
Is there a wish or purpose? Add an infinitive phrase: bhattaṃ pacituṃ icchati.
Need to describe a noun by what it is doing? Put a participle phrase directly before it, matching case and number: bhattaṃ pacantaṃ purisaṃ.

items.english: Having gone home, the man eats rice.
The man wishes to cook rice.
The doctor sees the man who is cooking rice.

items: A gerund shares its subject with the main verb and describes an earlier action.
Gerund and infinitive never change: plural subjects only change the main verb.
-tvā looks back (gantvā = having gone); -tuṃ looks forward (gantuṃ = to go).
Use the infinitive with icchati, ussahati, ārabhati, sakkoti and with verbs of motion to show purpose.
A participle must agree with its noun in gender, number and case.
Don’t mix up the verb ending -nti (“they cook”) with the participle -nto (“cooking”).
Some verbs are irregular: disvā (having seen), daṭṭhuṃ (to see), bhutvā (having eaten).

items.english: Having drunk water, the boys sleep. (gerund)
Having left the city, the merchants go to the village. (gerund with prefix)
The child comes home to drink water. (infinitive of purpose)
The farmer tries to plough the field. (infinitive with ussahati)

items.pali: Kassako khettaṃ kasantena puttena saddhiṃ bhāsati.
items.english: The farmer talks with the son who is ploughing the field. (participle, instrumental)

items.why: The gerund never takes a plural ending.
The gerund comes before the main verb.

items.wrong: Naro bhattaṃ khāditvā gehaṃ gacchati (meaning “goes home to eat”).
items.why: For a goal use -tuṃ; -tvā says the eating already happened.
The participle must be Accusative to describe purisaṃ.

items: Gerund and infinitive are fixed forms; the participle agrees like an adjective.
Order events as they happen: gerund phrases first, main verb last.
Participles describe a noun by what it is doing and must match its case and number.
Chapter 1’s case endings are the foundation for agreement.
